On the Sum of Element Orders in Finite Abelian Groups

Mohsen Amiri Address: Faculdade de Matemática, Universidade Federal de Uberlândia, Av. J. N. Ávila 2121, 38408-902 Uberlândia - MG, Brazil. Email address: m.amiri77@gmail.com
Abstract.

Let ψ⁡(G)=∑g∈Go⁡(g)\psi(G)=\sum_{g\in G}o(g) denote the sum of element orders of a finite group GG. It is known that among groups of order nn, the cyclic group CnC_{n} maximizes ψ\psi. Tărnăuceanu proved that two finite abelian pp-groups of the same order are isomorphic if and only if they have the same sum of element orders, and conjectured this for arbitrary finite abelian groups. In this paper, we confirm the conjecture by proving a stronger result: for finite L​C​MLCM-groups GG and HH of the same order, ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H) if and only if GG and HH have the same order type.

Key words and phrases: 
Finite nilpotent groups, pp-groups, Finite abelian groups.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
20D15 , 20K01

1. Introduction

In [3], H. Amiri, S. M. J. Amiri, and M. Isaacs introduced a new perspective on the spectrum of a finite group GG by defining the sum-of-element-orders function

ψ⁡(G)=∑g∈Go⁡(g)=∑m∈ω⁡(G)m⋅s⁡(m),\psi(G)=\sum_{g\in G}o(g)=\sum_{m\in\omega(G)}m\cdot s(m),

where ω⁡(G)\omega(G) denotes the set of element orders of GG, and s⁡(m)s(m) is the number of elements of order mm. They proved that among all groups of a given order nn, the cyclic group CnC_{n} maximizes this function, that is,

ψ⁡(Cn)=max⁡{ψ⁡(G):|G|=n}.\psi(C_{n})=\max\{\psi(G):|G|=n\}.

Subsequently, other authors (see [10]), and independently R. Shen, G. Chen, and C. Wu in [17], investigated groups attaining the second-largest value of ψ\psi. The function ψ\psi has since been studied extensively (see [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16, 18]). While some works focus on determining maximal, second-largest, or minimal values of ψ\psi, others establish structural criteria for finite groups, such as solvability or nilpotency, using this invariant. More recently, H. K. Dey and A. Mondal [15] obtained an exact upper bound for the sum of powers of element orders in non-cyclic finite groups.

To further understand the behavior of ψ\psi in special classes of groups, we focus on L​C​MLCM-groups. For a periodic group GG, define

LCM(G)={x∈G:o(xny)∣lcm(o(xn),o(y)) for all y∈G,n∈ℤ}.LCM(G)=\{x\in G:o(x^{n}y)\mid\mathrm{lcm}(o(x^{n}),o(y))\text{ for all }y\in G,\,n\in\mathbb{Z}\}.

A group GG is called an L​C​MLCM-group if G=L​C​M​(G)G=LCM(G). Every abelian group is an L​C​MLCM-group. By Theorem 2.6 of [1], every finite L​C​MLCM-group is nilpotent. Every regular or powerful pp-group is an L​C​MLCM-group. Furthermore, there exist numerous irregular pp-groups that are also L​C​MLCM-groups.

In [20], Tărnăuceanu proved that two finite abelian pp-groups of the same order are isomorphic if and only if they have the same sum of element orders. He further conjectured:

Conjecture 1.1.

Two finite abelian groups of the same order are isomorphic if and only if they have the same ψ\psi-value.

For any non-empty subset XX of a finite group GG, the exponent of XX, denoted exp⁡(X)\exp(X), is the smallest positive integer nn such that xn=1x^{n}=1 for all x∈Xx\in X.

Note that if GG and HH are two finite abelian pp-groups of the same order, and GG is a pp-group with exp⁡(G)>exp⁡(H)\exp(G)>\exp(H), then by Proposition 2.15 we have ψ⁡(G)>ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)>\psi(H). This monotonicity property of finite abelian pp-groups is essential in the proof of Conjecture 1.1 within the class of abelian pp-groups. However, this result cannot be extended to the wider class of all finite groups. For instance, let

G=C180×C5andH=C150×C6.G=C_{180}\times C_{5}\quad\text{and}\quad H=C_{150}\times C_{6}.

Then

exp⁡(G)=180>150=exp⁡(H),\exp(G)=180>150=\exp(H),

but

ψ⁡(G)=81191<91175=ψ⁡(H).\psi(G)=81191<91175=\psi(H).

Recall that two finite groups have the same order type if they have the same number of elements of each possible order.

We first establish the following results for L​C​MLCM-groups.

Theorem 1.2.

Let N≤GN\leq G and M≤HM\leq H be finite L​C​MLCM-groups of the same order and suppose [G:N]=[H:M]=p[G:N]=[H:M]=p is a prime number. Assume ψ⁡(N)\psi(N) and ψ⁡(M)\psi(M) are minimal among all maximal subgroups of index pp of GG and HH, respectively. If ψ⁡(G∖N)>ψ⁡(H∖M)\psi(G\setminus N)>\psi(H\setminus M), then ψ⁡(G)>ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)>\psi(H).

Theorem 1.3.

Let GG and HH be finite L​C​MLCM-groups of the same order. Then ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H) if and only if GG and HH have the same order type.

Note that Conjecture 1.1 does not hold for L​C​MLCM-groups that are not abelian. Indeed, consider a non-abelian pp-group GG of order p3p^{3} and exponent pp. Then GG is an L​C​MLCM-group and satisfies

ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(Cp×Cp×Cp),\psi(G)=\psi(C_{p}\times C_{p}\times C_{p}),

even though

G≇Cp×Cp×Cp.G\not\cong C_{p}\times C_{p}\times C_{p}.

As a consequence of Theorem 1.3, we give an affirmative answer to Conjecture 1.1. More precisely, we prove:

Theorem 1.4.

Let GG and HH be two finite abelian groups of order nn. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    The invariant factors of GG and HH are the same.

  2. (ii)

    G≅HG\cong H.

  3. (iii)

    GG and HH have the same order type.

  4. (iv)

    ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H).

Theorem 1.4 shows that the sum-of-orders function ψ\psi provides a complete invariant for finite abelian groups: two groups have the same ψ\psi-value if and only if they are isomorphic. Thus, ψ\psi offers a practical numerical tool for classifying finite abelian groups. Let G=C2×D16G=C_{2}\times D_{16} and H=C4×Q8H=C_{4}\times Q_{8}. Then G≠L​C​M​(G)G\neq LCM(G), and ψ⁡(G)=119=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=119=\psi(H), but GG and HH do not have the same order type. Hence, in Theorem 1.3, the condition G=L​C​M​(G)G=LCM(G) is essential.

For any two positive integers nn and rr, let nrn_{r} denote the largest divisor of nn whose set of prime divisors coincides with that of rr, and let π⁡(n)\pi(n) denote the set of all prime divisors of nn. All other notation used in this paper is standard and primarily follows [13].

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the notation and recall some basic results that will be used throughout the paper. We summarize definitions related to element orders, exponents, and L​C​MLCM-groups, and we state known lemmas and properties that will be needed in the proofs of our main theorems.

Lemma 2.1.

Let GG be a finite group and v∈Gv\in G of order m​nmn where g​c​d​(m,n)=1gcd(m,n)=1. Then there exist a,b∈⟨v⟩a,b\in\langle v\rangle such that v=a​bv=ab, o⁡(a)=mo(a)=m and o⁡(b)=no(b)=n.

Proof.

We have ⟨v⟩=⟨vm⟩×⟨vn⟩\langle v\rangle=\langle v^{m}\rangle\times\langle v^{n}\rangle. Then there are integers ii and jj such that v=vm​i​vn​jv=v^{mi}v^{nj}. Then v=a​bv=ab where a=vm​ia=v^{mi} and b=vn​jb=v^{nj}. Since g​c​d​(o⁡(a),o⁡(b))=1gcd(o(a),o(b))=1, we have n​m=o⁡(v)=o⁡(a)​o​(b)nm=o(v)=o(a)o(b). Therefore o⁡(a)=no(a)=n and o⁡(b)=mo(b)=m.

∎

Lemma 2.2 (Lemma 2.4 of [4]).

For any two finite groups AA and BB, we have

ψ⁡(A×B)≤ψ⁡(A)​ψ​(B).\psi(A\times B)\leq\psi(A)\psi(B).

Moreover, equality holds if and only if gcd⁡(|A|,|B|)=1\gcd(|A|,|B|)=1.

Let GG be a finite group. For any subgroup H≤GH\leq G and any element x∈Gx\in G, denote by

x​H={x​h∣h∈H}xH=\{xh\mid h\in H\}

the left coset of HH determined by xx.

Moreover, for any nonempty subset X⊆GX\subseteq G, define

ψ⁡(X)=∑x∈Xo⁡(x).\psi(X)=\sum_{x\in X}o(x).

We need the following generalization of Lemma 2.2.

Lemma 2.3.

Let W=R×KW=R\times K be a finite group, and let A≤RA\leq R and B≤KB\leq K. Let v∈Rv\in R and w∈Kw\in K. Then

ψ⁡(v​w​A​B)≤ψ⁡(v​A)​ψ​(w​B).\psi(vwAB)\leq\,\psi(vA)\psi(wB).

Moreover, if gcd⁡(|K|,|R|)=1\gcd(|K|,|R|)=1, then equality holds.

Proof.

Let a∈Aa\in A and b∈Bb\in B. Then v​a∈Rva\in R and w​b∈Kwb\in K. Since [K,R]=1[K,R]=1, we have w​a=a​wwa=aw, so v​w​a​b=v​a​w​bvwab=vawb. Consequently, o⁡(v​w​a​b)=o⁡(v​a​w​b)o(vwab)=o(vawb). Thus,

o⁡(v​w​a​b)=o⁡(v​a​w​b)|l​c​m​(o⁡(v​a),o⁡(w​b))≤o⁡(v​a)​o​(w​b).o(vwab)=o(vawb)\mid lcm(o(va),o(wb))\leq o(va)o(wb).

Moreover if g​c​d​(o⁡(v​a),o⁡(w​b))=1gcd(o(va),o(wb))=1, then o⁡(v​a​w​b)=o⁡(v​a)​o​(w​b)o(vawb)=o(va)o(wb), and so the equality holds. It follows that

ψ⁡(v​A×w​B)=∑a∈A,b∈Bo⁡(v​a​w​b)≤∑a∈A,b∈Bo⁡(v​a)​o​(w​b)=ψ⁡(v​A)​ψ​(w​B).\psi(vA\times wB)=\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}o(vawb)\leq\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}o(va)o(wb)=\psi(vA)\psi(wB).

Furthermore, if g​c​d​(|R|,|K|)=1gcd(|R|,|K|)=1, then

∑a∈A,b∈Bo⁡(v​a​w​b)=∑a∈A,b∈Bo⁡(v​a)​o​(w​b),\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}o(vawb)=\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}o(va)o(wb),

so the equality holds.

∎

For a pp-group GG and an integer nn, we denote by

Ω(n)​(G)={x∈G∣xpn=1}\Omega_{(n)}(G)=\{\,x\in G\mid x^{p^{n}}=1\,\}

the set of elements of order dividing pnp^{n}, and by Ωn​(G)\Omega_{n}(G) the subgroup generated by Ω(n)​(G)\Omega_{(n)}(G). For simplicity, we denote by ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM} the the class of all finite L​C​MLCM-groups. We begin by studying the structure of finite L​C​MLCM-groups.

Remark 2.4.

Let GG be a finite pp-group such that

Ω(i)​(G)=Ωi​(G)for all integers ​i≥0.\Omega_{(i)}(G)=\Omega_{i}(G)\quad\text{for all integers }i\geq 0.

Let x,y∈Gx,y\in G. If o⁡(x)≠o⁡(y)o(x)\neq o(y), then

o⁡(x​y)=max⁡{o⁡(x),o⁡(y)}=lcm⁡(o⁡(x),o⁡(y)).o(xy)=\max\{o(x),o(y)\}=\mathrm{lcm}(o(x),o(y)).

Now assume that o⁡(x)=o⁡(y)=pio(x)=o(y)=p^{i} for some i≥0i\geq 0. Since Ω(i)​(G)=Ωi​(G)\Omega_{(i)}(G)=\Omega_{i}(G), it follows that

o⁡(x​y)|pi=lcm⁡(o⁡(x),o⁡(y)).o(xy)\mid p^{i}=\mathrm{lcm}(o(x),o(y)).

Hence,

o⁡(x​y)|lcm⁡(o⁡(x),o⁡(y)).o(xy)\mid\mathrm{lcm}(o(x),o(y)).

Therefore, every element x∈Gx\in G satisfies

o⁡(x​y)|lcm⁡(o⁡(x),o⁡(y))for all ​y∈G,o(xy)\mid\mathrm{lcm}(o(x),o(y))\quad\text{for all }y\in G,

which shows that x∈L​C​M​(G)x\in LCM(G). Consequently, G∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳ.G\in\mathcal{LCM}.

Lemma 2.5.

Let GG be a finite pp-group. Then GG is an L​C​MLCM-group if and only if

Ω(i)​(G)=Ωi​(G)for all positive integers ​i.\Omega_{(i)}(G)=\Omega_{i}(G)\quad\text{for all positive integers }i.
Proof.

First suppose GG is an L​C​MLCM-group, and let x,y∈Ω(i)​(G)x,y\in\Omega_{(i)}(G). Then we have

o⁡(x​y)​∣lcm⁡(o⁡(x),o⁡(y))∣​pi.o(xy)\mid\operatorname{lcm}(o(x),o(y))\mid p^{i}.

Thus x​y∈Ω(i)​(G)xy\in\Omega_{(i)}(G). This shows that Ω(i)​(G)\Omega_{(i)}(G) is closed under multiplication, hence

Ω(i)​(G)=Ωi​(G).\Omega_{(i)}(G)=\Omega_{i}(G).

Conversely, if Ω(i)​(G)=Ωi​(G)\Omega_{(i)}(G)=\Omega_{i}(G) for all ii, then by Remark 2.4 G∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\in\mathcal{LCM}. ∎

Remark 2.6.

Let G,W∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG,W\in\mathcal{LCM} and let H≤GH\leq G. Take h∈Hh\in H. Since G∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\in\mathcal{LCM}, for all g∈Gg\in G we have

o⁡(h​g)|lcm⁡(o⁡(h),o⁡(g)).o(hg)\mid\mathrm{lcm}(o(h),o(g)).

In particular, this holds for all g∈Hg\in H. Hence,

o⁡(h​g)|lcm⁡(o⁡(h),o⁡(g))for all ​g∈H,o(hg)\mid\mathrm{lcm}(o(h),o(g))\quad\text{for all }g\in H,

which shows that H∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳH\in\mathcal{LCM}. Therefore, the class ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM} is closed under taking subgroups.

Moreover, by Proposition 2.12 of [2], the class ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM} is also closed under direct products.

The following theorem classifies L​C​MLCM-groups.

Theorem 2.7.

Let GG be a finite group. Then GG is an L​C​MLCM-group if and only if GG is nilpotent and each Sylow subgroup of GG is an L​C​MLCM-group.

Proof.

First assume that G∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\in\mathcal{LCM}. Let pp be a prime divisor of |G||G|. Since G=L​C​M​(G)G=LCM(G), the set of all pp-elements of GG is a subgroup of GG. Hence, the Sylow pp-subgroup of GG is normal, and so GG is nilpotent.

Conversely, suppose GG is nilpotent and that each Sylow subgroup of GG is an L​C​MLCM-group. Since GG is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups, by Remark 2.6, it follows that GG itself is an L​C​MLCM-group. ∎

From now on, we will use without further reference the fact that finite L​C​MLCM-groups are nilpotent.

We next establish a structural property of L​C​MLCM-groups that relates the group to its subgroup of elements of bounded order and the corresponding quotient.

Proposition 2.8.

Let GG be a finite nilpotent group, and let

N={x∈G:xd=1},N=\{x\in G:x^{d}=1\},

where dd is a divisor of |G||G|. Then GG is an L​C​MLCM-group if and only if both GN\frac{G}{N} and NN are L​C​MLCM-groups.

Proof.

Since GG is nilpotent, we may assume that GG is a pp-group, and let d=pmd=p^{m}. Then N=Ωm​(G)N=\Omega_{m}(G). If exp⁡(G)|pm\exp(G)\mid p^{m}, the claim is trivial, so assume exp⁡(G)=pr∤pm\exp(G)=p^{r}\nmid p^{m}.

First, suppose that GG is an L​C​MLCM-group. For each 1≤i≤r−m1\leq i\leq r-m, we have

Ω(i)​(GN)=Ω(i+m)​(G)N,\Omega_{(i)}\left(\frac{G}{N}\right)=\frac{\Omega_{(i+m)}(G)}{N},

which is a subgroup of GN\frac{G}{N}. Hence GN\frac{G}{N} is an L​C​MLCM-group.

Conversely, assume that both GN\frac{G}{N} and NN are L​C​MLCM-groups. For each 1≤i≤r−m1\leq i\leq r-m, since

Ω(i)​(GN)=Ω(i+m)​(G)N\Omega_{(i)}\left(\frac{G}{N}\right)=\frac{\Omega_{(i+m)}(G)}{N}

is a subgroup of GN\frac{G}{N}, it follows that Ω(i+m)​(G)\Omega_{(i+m)}(G) is a subgroup of GG. Moreover, since NN is an L​C​MLCM-group, Ω(i)​(G)\Omega_{(i)}(G) is a subgroup of GG for all 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m. Therefore, Ω(i)​(G)\Omega_{(i)}(G) is a subgroup of GG for all 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r, and hence by Lemma 2.5, GG is an L​C​MLCM-group. ∎

We next recall a useful reduction formula for computing ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) in terms of the quotient by Ω1​(G)\Omega_{1}(G).

Lemma 2.9.

Let GG be a finite pp-group such that Ω1​(G)\Omega_{1}(G) is a subgroup of GG of order prp^{r} and exponent pp. Then

ψ⁡(G)=1−p+pr+1​ψ​(GΩ1​(G)).\psi(G)=1-p+p^{r+1}\psi\left(\frac{G}{\Omega_{1}(G)}\right).
Proof.

Let N:=Ω1​(G)N:=\Omega_{1}(G). Then for every 1≠x∈G1\neq x\in G, we have ⟨x⟩∩N≠1\langle x\rangle\cap N\neq 1, since ⟨xo⁡(x)/p⟩≤⟨x⟩∩N\langle x^{o(x)/p}\rangle\leq\langle x\rangle\cap N.

Let XX be a left transversal of NN in GG such that 1∈X1\in X. If 1≠x∈X1\neq x\in X, then o⁡(x)≥p2o(x)\geq p^{2}, since x∉Nx\notin N. For any y∈Ny\in N, we have o⁡(x​y​N)=o⁡(x​N)o(xyN)=o(xN). Since |⟨x⟩∩N|=p|\langle x\rangle\cap N|=p, we have o⁡(x)/p=o⁡(x​N).o(x)/p=o(xN). As x∉Nx\not\in N, we have x​y∉Nxy\not\in N. Then

o⁡(x​y)=o⁡(x​y​N)⋅p=o⁡(x​N)⋅p=o⁡(x).o(xy)=o(xyN)\cdot p=o(xN)\cdot p=o(x).

Therefore

ψ⁡(G)=∑x∈Xψ⁡(x​N)=ψ⁡(N)+|N|​∑1≠x∈Xo⁡(x).\psi(G)=\sum_{x\in X}\psi(xN)=\psi(N)+|N|\sum_{1\neq x\in X}o(x).

Since for x∈X∖{1}x\in X\setminus\{1\}, we have ⟨x⟩∩N≠1\langle x\rangle\cap N\neq 1, it follows that o⁡(x)=p​o​(x​N)o(x)=p\,o(xN). Moreover,

ψ⁡(N)=1+(pr−1)​p=1−p+pr+1.\psi(N)=1+(p^{r}-1)p=1-p+p^{r+1}.

Hence,

ψ⁡(G)\displaystyle\psi(G) =ψ⁡(N)+|N|​∑1≠x∈Xo⁡(x)\displaystyle=\psi(N)+|N|\sum_{1\neq x\in X}o(x)
=ψ⁡(N)+|N|​p​∑1≠x∈Xo⁡(x​N)\displaystyle=\psi(N)+|N|p\sum_{1\neq x\in X}o(xN)
=ψ⁡(N)+pr+1​(ψ⁡(GN)−1)\displaystyle=\psi(N)+p^{r+1}\big(\psi\left(\frac{G}{N}\right)-1\big)
=1−p+pr+1​ψ​(GN),\displaystyle=1-p+p^{r+1}\psi\left(\frac{G}{N}\right),

as required. ∎

Remark 2.10.

Let PP be a finite pp-group. For any g∈G∖{1}g\in G\setminus\{1\}, we have p|o⁡(g).p\mid o(g). Then there exists a positive integer kk such that

ψ⁡(G)=∑g∈Go⁡(g)=1+∑g∈G∖{1}o⁡(g)=1+k​p.\psi(G)=\sum_{g\in G}o(g)=1+\sum_{g\in G\setminus\{1\}}o(g)=1+kp.

Consequently, p∤ψ⁡(G).p\nmid\psi(G).

In the following lemmas, we investigate some fundamental properties concerning the order of a product of several elements in an L​C​MLCM-group.

Let M≤GM\leq G be a subgroup and x∈Gx\in G. We define

o⁡(x,M):=min⁡{o⁡(x​g):g∈M}.o(x,M):=\min\{\,o(xg):g\in M\,\}.

Let GG be a finite group of order pm​np^{m}n, where pp is a prime number such that gcd⁡(p,n)=1\gcd(p,n)=1. By Lemma 2.1, for every element g∈Gg\in G, there exist commuting elements a,b∈Ga,b\in G such that

g=ab=ba,o(a)∣pm,ando(b)∣n.g=ab=ba,\quad o(a)\mid p^{m},\quad\text{and}\quad o(b)\mid n.

Throughout the sequel, we denote these elements by gp:=ag_{p}:=a and gp′:=bg_{p^{\prime}}:=b. Also, we denote by Gp′G_{p^{\prime}} any Hall p′p^{\prime}-subgroup of a finite nilpotent group GG.

Lemma 2.11.

Let G≤A∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\leq A\in\mathcal{LCM}. Suppose v∈Av\in A satisfies o⁡(v)=o⁡(v,G).o(v)=o(v,G). Then:

  1. (i)

    If w∈Aw\in A is a pp-element such that o⁡(w)≠o⁡(vp)o(w)\neq o(v_{p}), then o⁡(v​w)=l​c​m​(o⁡(v),o⁡(w)).o(vw)=lcm(o(v),o(w)).

  2. (ii)

    For all g∈Gg\in G, we have

    o⁡(v​g)=lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(g)).o(vg)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(g)).
Proof.

(i) Let P∈S​y​lp​(A)P\in Syl_{p}(A). Let o⁡(w)=pmo(w)=p^{m}, and let o⁡(vp)=pro(v_{p})=p^{r}. If r>mr>m, then vp​w∈P∖Ωr−1​(P)v_{p}w\in P\setminus\Omega_{r-1}(P) because AA is a nilpotent group, and so pr|o⁡(vp​w)p^{r}\mid o(v_{p}w). Since o⁡(vp​w)|l​c​m​(o⁡(vp),o⁡(w))o(v_{p}w)\mid lcm(o(v_{p}),o(w)), we have o⁡(v​w)=l​c​m​(o⁡(v),o⁡(w)).o(vw)=lcm(o(v),o(w)).

If r<mr<m, then vp​w∈P∖Ωm−1​(P)v_{p}w\in P\setminus\Omega_{m-1}(P), and similarly, we have the result.

(ii) Let g∈Gg\in G. First, we show that o⁡(v)|o⁡(v​g)o(v)\mid o(vg). Write A=P1×⋯×PkA=P_{1}\times\cdots\times P_{k}, where each Pi∈Sylpi​(A)P_{i}\in\mathrm{Syl}_{p_{i}}(A). Let v=v1⋯vkv=v_{1}\cdots v_{k} and g=g1⋯gkg=g_{1}\cdots g_{k}, with vi,gi∈Piv_{i},g_{i}\in P_{i} for all ii.

If, for some ii, we had o⁡(vi​gi)<o⁡(vi)o(v_{i}g_{i})<o(v_{i}), then

o⁡(v​gi)<o⁡(v)=o⁡(v,G),o(vg_{i})<o(v)=o(v,G),

a contradiction. Hence o⁡(vi)|o⁡(vi​gi)o(v_{i})\mid o(v_{i}g_{i}) for all ii, so o⁡(v)|o⁡(v​g)o(v)\mid o(vg).

Now we show that o⁡(v​g)=lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(g))o(vg)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(g)). By the above argument, it suffices to consider the case when AA is a pp-group.

If o⁡(g)=o⁡(v)o(g)=o(v), then

o⁡(v)|o⁡(v​g)|l​c​m​(o⁡(v),o⁡(g))=o⁡(v).o(v)\mid o(vg)\mid lcm(o(v),o(g))=o(v).

Thus

o⁡(v​g)=o⁡(v)=lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(g)).o(vg)=o(v)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(g)).

If o⁡(g)≠o⁡(v)o(g)\neq o(v), then we have the result by Case (i).

∎

Lemma 2.12.

Let A∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳA\in\mathcal{LCM} and GG a subgroup of AA. Suppose v∈Av\in A satisfies o⁡(v)=o⁡(v,G).o(v)=o(v,G). Let MM be a maximal subgroup of GG of index pp, and let w∈G∖Mw\in G\setminus M be a pp-element such that o⁡(w)=o⁡(w,M)o(w)=o(w,M). Then

o⁡(v​w)=o⁡(v​w,M).o(vw)=o(vw,M).
Proof.

We argue by induction on |A||A|.

Case 1. Assume first that AA is a pp-group. Let g∈Mg\in M be such that o⁡(v​w​g)<o⁡(v​w)o(vwg)<o(vw). Write o⁡(v​w)=pmo(vw)=p^{m}. If o⁡(v)=1o(v)=1, then v=1v=1, and hence

o⁡(v​w)=o⁡(w)=o⁡(w,M)=o⁡(v​w,M).o(vw)=o(w)=o(w,M)=o(vw,M).

Thus o⁡(v)≥po(v)\geq p, and consequently v∉Gv\notin G. Since p|o⁡(v​g)p\mid o(vg), we have

p≤o⁡(v​w​g)<o⁡(v​w),p\leq o(vwg)<o(vw),

and therefore m≥2m\geq 2. If o⁡(v​w​g)=1o(vwg)=1, then v=g−1​w−1∈Mv=g^{-1}w^{-1}\in M, which is impossible. Hence o⁡(v​w​g)≥po(vwg)\geq p. Let S=Ω1​(A)S=\Omega_{1}(A). Then

o⁡(v​S)=min⁡{o⁡(v​h​S):h∈G}ando⁡(w​S)=min⁡{o⁡(w​h​S):h∈M}.o(vS)=\min\{\,o(vhS):h\in G\,\}\quad\text{and}\quad o(wS)=\min\{\,o(whS):h\in M\,\}.

By the induction hypothesis,

o⁡(v​w​S)=min⁡{o⁡(v​w​h​S):h∈M}.o(vwS)=\min\{\,o(vwhS):h\in M\,\}.

In particular, o⁡(v​w​S)≤o⁡(v​w​g​S)o(vwS)\leq o(vwgS), which would imply o⁡(v​w)≤o⁡(v​w​g)o(vw)\leq o(vwg), a contradiction.

Case 2. Now assume that AA is not a pp-group. Write A=P1×⋯×PkA=P_{1}\times\cdots\times P_{k}, where each Pi∈Sylpi​(A)P_{i}\in\mathrm{Syl}_{p_{i}}(A). Let v=v1⋯vkv=v_{1}\cdots v_{k} and g=g1⋯gkg=g_{1}\cdots g_{k}, with vi,gi∈Piv_{i},g_{i}\in P_{i} for all ii.

Suppose, for some ii, that o⁡(vi​hi)<o⁡(vi)o(v_{i}h_{i})<o(v_{i}) for some hi∈Pih_{i}\in P_{i}. Then

o⁡(v​hi)<o⁡(v)=o⁡(v,G),o(vh_{i})<o(v)=o(v,G),

a contradiction. Hence o⁡(vi)≤o⁡(vi​hi)o(v_{i})\leq o(v_{i}h_{i}) for all hi∈Pih_{i}\in P_{i}, and therefore o⁡(vi)=o⁡(vi,Pi)o(v_{i})=o(v_{i},P_{i}). Without loss of generality, assume p=p1p=p_{1}.

By the induction hypothesis applied to ⟨P1,v1⟩\langle P_{1},v_{1}\rangle, we have

o⁡(v1​w)=o⁡(v1​w,P1∩M).o(v_{1}w)=o(v_{1}w,P_{1}\cap M).

Consequently,

o⁡(v​w)=o⁡(v​w,M).o(vw)=o(vw,M).

∎

Let GG and HH be two finite groups. We say that a subset XX of GG and a subset YY of HH have the same order type if, for every positive integer nn, the number of elements of order nn in XX is equal to the number of elements of order nn in YY.

Lemma 2.13.

Let G≤A∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\leq A\in\mathcal{LCM}, and let v,w∈Av,w\in A be such that

o⁡(v,G)=o⁡(v)ando⁡(v​w,G)=o⁡(v​w)=lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(w)).o(v,G)=o(v)\quad\text{and}\quad o(vw,G)=o(vw)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(w)).

Let

B=⟨v⟩×⟨w⟩×G.B=\langle v\rangle\times\langle w\rangle\times G.

Then (v,w,G)={(v,w,g):g∈G}(v,w,G)=\{(v,w,g):g\in G\} and v​w​GvwG have the same order type.

Proof.

Define f:v​w​G→(v,w,G)f:vwG\to(v,w,G) by f⁡(v​w​g)=(v,w,g)f(vwg)=(v,w,g) for all g∈Gg\in G. Let g∈Gg\in G. Then by Lemma 2.11,

o⁡(v​w​g)\displaystyle o(vwg) =lcm⁡(o⁡(v​w),o⁡(g))\displaystyle=\operatorname{lcm}(o(vw),o(g))
=lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(w),o⁡(g))\displaystyle=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(w),o(g))
=o⁡((,,,,,))\displaystyle=o((v,w,g))
=o⁡(f⁡(v​w​g)).\displaystyle=o(f(vwg)).

Hence, (v,w,G)(v,w,G) and v​w​GvwG have the same order type.

∎

The following lemma provides a relation between the order types of corresponding cosets of a maximal subgroup in an ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM}-group.

Lemma 2.14.

Let M≤G≤A∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳM\leq G\leq A\in\mathcal{LCM} where MM is a maximal subgroup of GG. Let v∈Av\in A and x∈G∖Mx\in G\setminus M satisfy o⁡(v)=o⁡(v,G)o(v)=o(v,G) and o⁡(v​x,M)=o⁡(v​x)o(vx,M)=o(vx). Then, for every integer 1≤i≤[G:M]−11\leq i\leq[G:M]-1, the cosets v​x​MvxM and v​xi​Mvx^{i}M have the same order type. In particular,

ψ⁡(v​x​M)=ψ⁡(v​xi​M).\psi(vxM)=\psi(vx^{i}M).
Proof.

By Lemma 2.12, o⁡(v​x)=o⁡(v​x,M)o(vx)=o(vx,M) and by Lemma 2.11, o⁡(v​x)=lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(x))o(vx)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(x)), as o⁡(v,G)=o⁡(v)o(v,G)=o(v). By Lemma 2.13, we may assume without loss of generality that A=⟨v⟩×⟨x⟩×MA=\langle v\rangle\times\langle x\rangle\times M.

Hence, for any g∈Mg\in M, we have

o⁡(v​x​h)\displaystyle o(vxh) =lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(x),o⁡(h))\displaystyle=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(x),o(h))
=lcm⁡(o⁡(v),o⁡(xi),o⁡(h))\displaystyle=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v),o(x^{i}),o(h))
=o⁡(v​xi​h).\displaystyle=o(vx^{i}h).

Define

f:v​x​M⟶v​xi​M,byf⁡(v​x​g)=v​xi​g.f:vxM\longrightarrow vx^{i}M,\quad\text{by}\quad f(vxg)=vx^{i}g.

Then o⁡(v​x​g)=o⁡(v​xi​g)o(vxg)=o(vx^{i}g) for all g∈Mg\in M, so the cosets v​x​MvxM and v​xi​Mvx^{i}M have the same order type. Consequently,

ψ⁡(v​x​M)=∑h∈Mo⁡(v​x​h)=∑h∈Mo⁡(v​xi​h)=ψ⁡(v​xi​M).∎\psi(vxM)=\sum_{h\in M}o(vxh)=\sum_{h\in M}o(vx^{i}h)=\psi(vx^{i}M).\qed

We now prove a fundamental monotonicity property of the function ψ\psi within a certain class of finite pp-groups.

Proposition 2.15.

Let P,Q∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳP,Q\in\mathcal{LCM} be finite pp-groups of the same order. If exp⁡(P)>exp⁡(Q)\exp(P)>\exp(Q), then

ψ⁡(P)≥(p−1)​ψ​(Q).\psi(P)\geq(p-1)\psi(Q).
Proof.

Let |P|=pn|P|=p^{n} and e​x​p​(P)=pmexp(P)=p^{m}. Since Ωm−1​(P)\Omega_{m-1}(P) is a proper subgroup of PP, we have

|P∖Ωm−1​(P)|≥pn−pn−1.|P\setminus\Omega_{m-1}(P)|\geq p^{n}-p^{n-1}.

For any x∈P∖Ωm−1​(P)x\in P\setminus\Omega_{m-1}(P), we have o⁡(x)=pmo(x)=p^{m}. Since e​x​p​(P)=pm>pm−1≥e​x​p​(Q)exp(P)=p^{m}>p^{m-1}\geq exp(Q), we have

ψ⁡(Q)=∑g∈Qo⁡(g)<pm−1​|Q|=pm−1​pn\psi(Q)=\sum_{g\in Q}o(g)<p^{m-1}|Q|=p^{m-1}p^{n}

Then

ψ⁡(P)\displaystyle\psi(P) =∑x∈P∖Ωm−1​(P)o⁡(x)+ψ⁡(Ωm−1​(P))\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in P\setminus\Omega_{m-1}(P)}o(x)+\psi(\Omega_{m-1}(P))
>∑x∈P∖Ωm−1​(P)o⁡(x)\displaystyle>\sum_{x\in P\setminus\Omega_{m-1}(P)}o(x)
≥(pn−pn−1)​pm\displaystyle\geq(p^{n}-p^{n-1})p^{m}
≥(p−1)​pn​pm−1\displaystyle\geq(p-1)p^{n}p^{m-1}
≥(p−1)​ψ​(Q).\displaystyle\geq(p-1)\psi(Q).

∎

Lemma 2.16.

Let G∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\in\mathcal{LCM} be a finite pp-group, and let H=Cpm×(Cp)n−mH=C_{p^{m}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m} such that |G|=|H||G|=|H|. If e​x​p​(G)≥pmexp(G)\geq p^{m}, then there exists a bijection f:H→Gf:H\to G such that o⁡(h)|o⁡(f⁡(h))o(h)\mid o(f(h)) for all h∈Hh\in H.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on mm.

First suppose m=1m=1. Let ff be any bijection from HH onto GG such that f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1. Then for any h∈H∖{1}h\in H\setminus\{1\}, we have o⁡(h)=p=o⁡(f⁡(h))o(h)=p=o(f(h)).

So suppose that m>1m>1. Let MM be a maximal subgroup of GG such that Ωm−1​(G)≤M\Omega_{m-1}(G)\leq M. By the induction hypothesis, there exists a bijection β:Cpm−1×(Cp)n−m→M\beta:C_{p^{m-1}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m}\to M such that o⁡(h)|o⁡(β⁡(h))o(h)\mid o(\beta(h)) for all h∈Cpm−1×(Cp)n−mh\in C_{p^{m-1}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m}. We may assume that Cpm−1×(Cp)n−m≤Cpm×(Cp)n−mC_{p^{m-1}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m}\leq C_{p^{m}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m}. Let z∈Cpm×(Cp)n−m∖Cpm−1×(Cp)n−mz\in C_{p^{m}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m}\setminus C_{p^{m-1}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m} and x∈G∖Mx\in G\setminus M. Then pm=o⁡(z​h)p^{m}=o(zh), and o⁡(x​g)=o⁡(x)o(xg)=o(x) for all h∈Cpm−1×(Cp)n−mh\in C_{p^{m-1}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m} and g∈Mg\in M. Let

η:(Cpm×(Cp)n−m)∖(Cpm−1×(Cp)n−m)→G∖M,\eta:(C_{p^{m}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m})\setminus(C_{p^{m-1}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m})\to G\setminus M,

be any bijection.

Then f=β∪ηf=\beta\cup\eta is a bijection from HH to GG such that o⁡(h)|o⁡(f⁡(h))o(h)\mid o(f(h)) for all h∈Hh\in H. ∎

The following lemma is useful to prove Lemma 3.4.

Lemma 2.17.

Let G≤A∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\leq A\in\mathcal{LCM} be finite pp-groups and let MM be a maximal subgroups of GG such that e​x​p​(M)=e​x​p​(G)exp(M)=exp(G). Let v∈Av\in A such that o⁡(v)=o⁡(v,G)o(v)=o(v,G). Then for any x∈G∖Mx\in G\setminus M, we have

p+1p​ψ​(v​M)>ψ⁡(v​x​M).\frac{p+1}{p}\psi(vM)>\psi(vxM).
Proof.

We proceed by induction on |G||G|. We may assume that o⁡(x​M)=o⁡(x,M)o(xM)=o(x,M). If o⁡(v)≥o⁡(x)o(v)\geq o(x), then for any g∈Mg\in M by Lemmas 2.11 (ii) and Lemma 2.12, we have

o⁡(v​x​g)=l​c​m​(o⁡(v),o⁡(x​g))=l​c​m​(o⁡(v),o⁡(x),o⁡(g))=l​c​m​(o⁡(v),o⁡(g))=o⁡(v​g).o(vxg)=lcm(o(v),o(xg))=lcm(o(v),o(x),o(g))=lcm(o(v),o(g))=o(vg).

Thus,

ψ⁡(v​x​M)=∑g∈Mo⁡(v​x​g)=∑g∈Mo⁡(v​g)=ψ⁡(v​M).\psi(vxM)=\sum_{g\in M}o(vxg)=\sum_{g\in M}o(vg)=\psi(vM).

Hence,

p+1p​ψ​(v​x​M)=p+1p​ψ​(v​M)>ψ⁡(v​M).\frac{p+1}{p}\psi(vxM)=\frac{p+1}{p}\psi(vM)>\psi(vM).

So o⁡(v)<o⁡(x)o(v)<o(x). Therefore ψ⁡(v​x​M)=ψ⁡(x​M)\psi(vxM)=\psi(xM).

If e​x​p​(G)=pexp(G)=p, then o⁡(v)=1o(v)=1, so ψ⁡(v​x​M)=p​|M|\psi(vxM)=p|M| and ψ⁡(v​M)=pn+1−p+1\psi(vM)=p^{n+1}-p+1 where |M|=pn|M|=p^{n}. Since

p+1p​(pn+1−p+1)>pn,\frac{p+1}{p}(p^{n+1}-p+1)>p^{n},

we have

p+1p​ψ​(M)>ψ⁡(x​M).\frac{p+1}{p}\psi(M)>\psi(xM).

So e​x​p​(G):=pm>pexp(G):=p^{m}>p.

By Lemma 2.16, there exists a bijection ff from Cpm×(Cp)n−mC_{p^{m}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m} onto MM such that o⁡(g)|o⁡(f⁡(g))o(g)\mid o(f(g)) for all g∈Gg\in G. Then ψ⁡(M)≥ψ⁡(Cpm×(Cp)n−m)\psi(M)\geq\psi(C_{p^{m}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m}).

By Lemma 2.9,

ψ⁡(Cpm×(Cp)n−m)=1−p+pn−m+2​p2​m−1+1p+1.\psi(C_{p^{m}}\times(C_{p})^{n-m})=1-p+p^{n-m+2}\frac{p^{2m-1}+1}{p+1}.

Since

p+1p​(1−p+pn−m+2​p2​m−1+1p+1)>pn+m=ψ⁡(v​x​M),\frac{p+1}{p}(1-p+p^{n-m+2}\frac{p^{2m-1}+1}{p+1})>p^{n+m}=\psi(vxM),

we have

p+1p​ψ​(v​M)≥p+1p​ψ​(M)>ψ⁡(v​x​M).\frac{p+1}{p}\psi(vM)\geq\frac{p+1}{p}\psi(M)>\psi(vxM).

∎

We also require the following lemma, which establishes a relation between the orders of elements in consecutive layers of a finite L​C​MLCM-group.

Lemma 2.18.

Let M≤G≤AM\leq G\leq A be finite L​C​MLCM-groups, where MM is a maximal subgroup of GG of index pp, chosen such that ψ⁡(v​M)\psi(vM) is minimal among all maximal subgroups of index pp in GG for some v∈Av\in A. Then, for any x∈G∖Mx\in G\setminus M, we have

(o⁡(v​x))p=(exp⁡(v​G))p.\big(o(vx)\big)_{p}=\big(\exp(vG)\big)_{p}.
Proof.

Write G=P×KG=P\times K, where P∈Sylp​(G)P\in\mathrm{Syl}_{p}(G) and KK is a Hall p′p^{\prime}-subgroup of GG. Since x​M=xp​MxM=x_{p}M, we may assume x=xpx=x_{p}. For any maximal subgroup LL of GG of index pp we have K≤LK\leq L (hence K≤MK\leq M). By Lemma 2.3,

ψ⁡(v​M)=ψ⁡(vp​(P∩M))​ψ​(vp′​K)≤ψ⁡(vp​(P∩L))​ψ​(vp′​K).\psi(vM)=\psi\big(v_{p}(P\cap M)\big)\,\psi(v_{p^{\prime}}K)\leq\psi\big(v_{p}(P\cap L)\big)\,\psi(v_{p^{\prime}}K).

Therefore ψ⁡(vp​(P∩M))≤ψ⁡(vp​(P∩L))\psi\big(v_{p}(P\cap M)\big)\leq\psi\big(v_{p}(P\cap L)\big) for every such LL, and consequently we may assume K=1K=1 (and vp′=1v_{p^{\prime}}=1), so G=PG=P.

If o⁡(v)=exp⁡(v​G)o(v)=\exp(vG), then by Lemma 2.11 we have

o⁡(v​x)=exp⁡(v​G),o(vx)=\exp(vG),

and we are done.

So suppose o⁡(v)<exp⁡(v​G)o(v)<\exp(vG). For a contradiction assume

o⁡(v​x):=pm<exp⁡(v​G):=pr.o(vx):=p^{m}<\exp(vG):=p^{r}.

Let RR be a maximal subgroup of GG of index pp such that Ωr−1​(P)≤R\Omega_{r-1}(P)\leq R. Since x∉Ωr−1​(M∩P)x\notin\Omega_{r-1}(M\cap P) we have

|Ωr−1​(M∩P)|​p≤|Ωr−1​(P)|.|\Omega_{r-1}(M\cap P)|\,p\leq|\Omega_{r-1}(P)|.

Then

ψ⁡(v​R)\displaystyle\psi(vR) =o⁡(v)​[(|R|−|Ωr−1​(G)|)​pr+ψ⁡(o⁡(v)​Ωr−1​(G))]\displaystyle=o(v)\big[(|R|-|\Omega_{r-1}(G)|)p^{r}+\psi(o(v)\,\Omega_{r-1}(G))\big]
<o⁡(v)​[(|M|−|Ωr−1​(M)|)​pr+ψ⁡(o⁡(v)​Ωr−1​(M))]\displaystyle<o(v)\big[(|M|-|\Omega_{r-1}(M)|)p^{r}+\psi(o(v)\,\Omega_{r-1}(M))\big]
=ψ⁡(v​M),\displaystyle=\psi(vM),

a contradiction. ∎

3. Main Results

First we prove our main results for finite pp-groups which are L​C​MLCM-groups.

Lemma 3.1.

Let G,H∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG,H\in\mathcal{LCM} be finite pp-groups of the same order. Then ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H) if and only if GG and HH have the same order type.

Proof.

Suppose ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H). We proceed by induction on |G||G|.

By Proposition 2.15, e​x​p​(G)=e​x​p​(H):=pmexp(G)=exp(H):=p^{m}. Let N=Ω1​(P)N=\Omega_{1}(P) and D=Ω1​(Q)D=\Omega_{1}(Q). If m=1m=1, then clearly, G=NG=N and H=DH=D have the same order type.

So m>1m>1. Since GG and HH are L​C​MLCM-groups, e​x​p​(N)=e​x​p​(D)=pexp(N)=exp(D)=p. By Lemma 2.9,

1−p+|N|p​ψ​(GN)=ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)=1−p+|D|​p​ψ​(HD).1-p+|N|p\psi\left(\frac{G}{N}\right)=\psi(G)=\psi(H)=1-p+|D|p\psi\left(\frac{H}{D}\right).

Consequently,

|N|​p​ψ​(GN)=|D|​p​ψ​(HD).|N|p\psi\left(\frac{G}{N}\right)=|D|p\psi\left(\frac{H}{D}\right).

By Remark 2.10, p∤ψ⁡(GN)​ψ​(HD)p\nmid\psi\left(\frac{G}{N}\right)\psi\left(\frac{H}{D}\right). Therefore |N|​p=|D|​p|N|p=|D|p. By Proposition 2.8, GN\frac{G}{N} and HD\frac{H}{D} are L​C​MLCM-groups. By the induction hypothesis, GN\frac{G}{N} and HD\frac{H}{D} have the same order type. Let

f:GN⟶HDf:\frac{G}{N}\longrightarrow\frac{H}{D}

be a bijection such that

o⁡(f⁡(x​N))=o⁡(x​N)for all ​x​N∈GN.o\big(f(xN)\big)=o(xN)\quad\text{for all }xN\in\frac{G}{N}.

Let XX and YY be left transversals of NN in GG and DD in HH, respectively, chosen so that

o⁡(x,N)=o⁡(x)ando⁡(y,D)=o⁡(y)o(x,N)=o(x)\quad\text{and}\quad o(y,D)=o(y)

for all x∈Xx\in X and y∈Yy\in Y.

Let x∈X∖{1}x\in X\setminus\{1\}. Then there exists a unique y∈Yy\in Y such that

f⁡(x​N)=y​D.f(xN)=yD.

Since x∉Nx\notin N and y∉Dy\notin D, it follows that o⁡(x)>po(x)>p and o⁡(y)>po(y)>p.

Because GG and HH are L​C​MLCM-groups, we have

o⁡(x​g)=o⁡(x)ando⁡(y​h)=o⁡(y)o(xg)=o(x)\quad\text{and}\quad o(yh)=o(y)

for all g∈Ng\in N and h∈Dh\in D.

Moreover, since |N|=|D|=p|N|=|D|=p and o⁡(x​N)=o⁡(y​D)o(xN)=o(yD), we obtain

o⁡(x​g)=o⁡(x​N)⋅p=o⁡(y​D)⋅p=o⁡(y​h)o(xg)=o(xN)\cdot p=o(yD)\cdot p=o(yh)

for all g∈Ng\in N and h∈Dh\in D.

As NN and DD have the same order type, it follows that the cosets x​NxN and y​DyD determine the same order type in GG and HH, respectively. Hence GG and HH have the same order type.

The converse is straightforward.

∎

The following Corollary was established in [20]; we provide here a more concise proof for completeness.

Corollary 3.2.

Let PP and QQ be two abelian pp-groups of the same order. Then ψ⁡(P)=ψ⁡(Q)\psi(P)=\psi(Q) if and only if P≅QP\cong Q.

Proof.

If P≅QP\cong Q, then clearly ψ⁡(P)=ψ⁡(Q)\psi(P)=\psi(Q).

So suppose ψ⁡(P)=ψ⁡(Q)\psi(P)=\psi(Q). By Lemma 3.1, PP and QQ have the same order type, and so they have the same invariant factors. Consequently P≅QP\cong Q. ∎

Now we prove the result in a more general setting.

The next two lemmas are special cases of Theorem 3.6; they give a comparison between the sums of element orders of corresponding cosets in finite ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM}-groups.

Lemma 3.3.

Let G≤A∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\leq A\in\mathcal{LCM} and H≤B∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳH\leq B\in\mathcal{LCM} be finite groups with |G|=|H|=:n|G|=|H|=:n. Let v∈Av\in A and u∈Bu\in B satisfy

o⁡(v,G)=o⁡(v),o⁡(u,H)=o⁡(u),π⁡(o⁡(v))=π⁡(o⁡(u)).o(v,G)=o(v),\quad o(u,H)=o(u),\quad\pi(o(v))=\pi(o(u)).

Let w∈Aw\in A and z∈Bz\in B be pp-elements where π⁡(o⁡(w))=π⁡(o⁡(z))\pi(o(w))=\pi(o(z)),

o⁡(w,G)=o⁡(w),o⁡(vp​w)=o⁡(vp​w,G)=lcm⁡(o⁡(vp),o⁡(w))=(exp⁡(v​G))p,o(w,G)=o(w),\quad o(v_{p}w)=o(v_{p}w,G)=\mathrm{lcm}\big(o(v_{p}),o(w)\big)=\big(\exp(vG)\big)_{p},
o⁡(z,H)=o⁡(z),o⁡(up​z)=o⁡(up​z,H)=lcm⁡(o⁡(up),o⁡(z))=(exp⁡(u​H))p.o(z,H)=o(z),\quad o(u_{p}z)=o(u_{p}z,H)=\mathrm{lcm}\big(o(u_{p}),o(z)\big)=\big(\exp(uH)\big)_{p}.

If ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H)\psi(vG)>\psi(uH), then ψ⁡(v​w​G)>ψ⁡(u​z​H)\psi(vwG)>\psi(uzH).

Moreover, let N≤GN\leq G and M≤HM\leq H be maximal subgroups of index pp where

exp⁡(v​N)=exp⁡(v​G),exp⁡(u​M)=exp⁡(u​H),\exp(vN)=\exp(vG),\quad\exp(uM)=\exp(uH),

and

ψ⁡(v​N)≤ψ⁡(v​R)andψ⁡(u​M)≤ψ⁡(u​E)\psi(vN)\leq\psi(vR)\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(uM)\leq\psi(uE)

for all maximal subgroups R≤GR\leq G and E≤HE\leq H. Let x∈G∖Nx\in G\setminus N and y∈H∖My\in H\setminus M satisfy o⁡(x,N)=o⁡(x)o(x,N)=o(x) and o⁡(y,M)=o⁡(y)o(y,M)=o(y). Then

ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H)if and only ifψ⁡(v​x​N)>ψ⁡(u​y​M).\psi(vG)>\psi(uH)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\psi(vxN)>\psi(uyM).
Proof.

We proceed by induction on |G||G|.

Base case: |G|=p|G|=p is prime.

Since π⁡(o⁡(v))=π⁡(o⁡(u))\pi(o(v))=\pi(o(u)), we deduce that p|o⁡(v)p\mid o(v) if and only if p|o⁡(u)p\mid o(u).

If p|o⁡(v)p\mid o(v), then by Lemma 2.11, o⁡(v​x)=o⁡(v)o(vx)=o(v) and o⁡(u​y)=o⁡(u)o(uy)=o(u). Also, by Lemma 2.11, o⁡(v​w)=o⁡(v)o(vw)=o(v) and o⁡(u​z)=o⁡(u)o(uz)=o(u).

If ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H)\psi(vG)>\psi(uH), then

ψ⁡(v​w​G)=ψ⁡(v​G)=p​o​(v)>p​o​(u)=ψ⁡(u​H)=ψ⁡(u​z​H).\psi(vwG)=\psi(vG)=p\,o(v)>p\,o(u)=\psi(uH)=\psi(uzH).

Also, since o⁡(v)>o⁡(u)o(v)>o(u), we have

ψ⁡(v​x​N)=o⁡(v​x)=o⁡(v)>o⁡(u)=o⁡(u​y)=ψ⁡(u​y​M).\psi(vxN)=o(vx)=o(v)>o(u)=o(uy)=\psi(uyM).

If ψ⁡(v​x​N)>ψ⁡(u​y​M)\psi(vxN)>\psi(uyM), then o⁡(v​x)>o⁡(u​y).o(vx)>o(uy). By Lemma 2.11, o⁡(v​x)=o⁡(v)o(vx)=o(v) and o⁡(u​y)=o⁡(u)o(uy)=o(u). Therefore

ψ⁡(v​G)=p​o​(v)>p​o​(u)=ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)=p\,o(v)>p\,o(u)=\psi(uH).

Now suppose p∤o⁡(v)p\nmid o(v); then p∤o⁡(u)p\nmid o(u) as well. By Lemma 2.11, o⁡(v​x)=p​o​(v)o(vx)=p\,o(v), o⁡(u​y)=p​o​(u)o(uy)=p\,o(u), o⁡(v​w)=p​o​(v)o(vw)=po(v) and o⁡(u​z)=p​o​(u)o(uz)=po(u).

If ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H)\psi(vG)>\psi(uH), then

ψ⁡(v​G)=[(p−1)​p+1]​o​(v)>[(p−1)​p+1]​o​(u)=ψ⁡(u​H),\psi(vG)=[(p-1)p+1]\,o(v)>[(p-1)p+1]\,o(u)=\psi(uH),

and hence o⁡(v)>o⁡(u)o(v)>o(u). Therefore,

ψ⁡(v​w​G)=p2​o​(v)>p2​o​(u)=ψ⁡(u​z​H).\psi(vwG)=p^{2}\,o(v)>p^{2}\,o(u)=\psi(uzH).

and

ψ⁡(v​x​N)=p​o​(v)>p​o​(u)=ψ⁡(u​y​M).\psi(vxN)=p\,o(v)>p\,o(u)=\psi(uyM).

If

ψ⁡(v​x​N)=o⁡(v​x)=p​o​(v)>ψ⁡(u​y​M)=o⁡(u​y)=p​o​(u),\psi(vxN)=o(vx)=po(v)>\psi(uyM)=o(uy)=po(u),

then o⁡(v)>o⁡(u)o(v)>o(u), so

ψ⁡(v​G)=[(p−1)​p+1]​o​(v)>[(p−1)​p+1]​o​(u)=ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)=[(p-1)p+1]o(v)>[(p-1)p+1]o(u)=\psi(uH).

Thus, the base case holds in both situations.

Inductive step: Assume |G|>p|G|>p and that the statement holds for smaller groups.

Suppose ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H)\psi(vG)>\psi(uH). We first show that ψ⁡(v​x​N)>ψ⁡(u​y​M)\psi(vxN)>\psi(uyM). Suppose, for a contradiction, that ψ⁡(v​x​N)≤ψ⁡(u​y​M)\psi(vxN)\leq\psi(uyM).

If ψ⁡(v​N)≤ψ⁡(u​M)\psi(vN)\leq\psi(uM), then

ψ⁡(v​G)=(p−1)​ψ​(v​x​N)+ψ⁡(v​N)≤(p−1)​ψ​(u​y​M)+ψ⁡(u​M)=ψ⁡(u​H),\psi(vG)=(p-1)\psi(vxN)+\psi(vN)\leq(p-1)\psi(uyM)+\psi(uM)=\psi(uH),

contradicting the hypothesis. Hence, ψ⁡(v​N)>ψ⁡(u​M)\psi(vN)>\psi(uM).

By Lemma 2.18, we have o⁡(vp​x)=(exp⁡(v​N))po(v_{p}x)=\big(\exp(vN)\big)_{p} and o⁡(up​y)=(exp⁡(u​M))po(u_{p}y)=\big(\exp(uM)\big)_{p}. Then, by Lemma 2.11,

o(vpx)=lcm(o(vp),o(x))=(exp(vN))p,o(upy)=lcm(o(up),o(y))=(exp(uM))p.o(v_{p}x)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v_{p}),o(x))=\big(\exp(vN)\big)_{p},\qquad o(u_{p}y)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(u_{p}),o(y))=\big(\exp(uM)\big)_{p}.

Let w1=xw_{1}=x and z1=yz_{1}=y. Since ψ⁡(v​N)>ψ⁡(u​M)\psi(vN)>\psi(uM) and |N|<|G||N|<|G|, by the induction hypothesis,

ψ⁡(v​x​N)=ψ⁡(v​w1​N)>ψ⁡(u​z1​N)=ψ⁡(u​y​M),\psi(vxN)=\psi(vw_{1}N)>\psi(uz_{1}N)=\psi(uyM),

a contradiction. Thus, ψ⁡(v​x​N)>ψ⁡(u​y​M)\psi(vxN)>\psi(uyM).

We now show that ψ⁡(v​w​G)>ψ⁡(u​z​H)\psi(vwG)>\psi(uzH). If w∈Gw\in G, then o⁡(w)=o⁡(w,G)=1o(w)=o(w,G)=1, so π⁡(o⁡(w))=∅\pi(o(w))=\varnothing. Since π⁡(o⁡(w))=π⁡(o⁡(z))\pi(o(w))=\pi(o(z)), we have 1=o⁡(z)=o⁡(z,H)1=o(z)=o(z,H), thus z∈Hz\in H. Then

ψ⁡(v​w​G)=ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H)=ψ⁡(u​z​H).\psi(vwG)=\psi(vG)>\psi(uH)=\psi(uzH).

So w∉Gw\not\in G and z∉Hz\not\in H. By Lemma 2.14, we may assume

[w,G]=[v,G]=[v,w]=1,[z,H]=[u,H]=[z,u]=1.[w,G]=[v,G]=[v,w]=1,\qquad[z,H]=[u,H]=[z,u]=1.

By Lemma 2.11,

o⁡(vp​x​w)=lcm⁡(o⁡(vp),o⁡(x),o⁡(w))=(exp⁡(v​N))pando(v_{p}xw)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(v_{p}),o(x),o(w))=\big(\exp(vN)\big)_{p}\quad\text{and}
o⁡(up​y​z)=lcm⁡(o⁡(up),o⁡(y),o⁡(z))=(exp⁡(u​M))p.o(u_{p}yz)=\operatorname{lcm}(o(u_{p}),o(y),o(z))=\big(\exp(uM)\big)_{p}.

Since ψ⁡(v​x​N)>ψ⁡(u​y​M)\psi(vxN)>\psi(uyM), by induction,

ψ⁡(v​x​w​N)>ψ⁡(u​y​z​M).\psi(vxwN)>\psi(uyzM).

Let P∈S​y​lp​(G)P\in Syl_{p}(G) and Q∈S​y​lp​(H)Q\in Syl_{p}(H). Since GG and HH are L​C​MLCM-groups, they are nilpotent, so

G=P×KandH=Q×F,G=P\times K\quad\text{and}\quad H=Q\times F,

where KK and FF are Hall p′p^{\prime}-subgroups of GG and HH, respectively. By Lemma 2.3,

ψ⁡(v​w​G)=ψ⁡(vp​w​P)​ψ​(vp′​K)andψ⁡(u​z​H)=ψ⁡(up​z​Q)​ψ​(up′​F),\psi(vwG)=\psi(v_{p}wP)\psi(v_{p^{\prime}}K)\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(uzH)=\psi(u_{p}zQ)\psi(u_{p^{\prime}}F),

Since o⁡(vp​x​w)=o⁡(vp​w)=(exp⁡(vp​G))po(v_{p}xw)=o(v_{p}w)=\big(\exp(v_{p}G)\big)_{p} and o⁡(up​y​z)=o⁡(up​z)=(exp⁡(u​H))p,o(u_{p}yz)=o(u_{p}z)=\big(\exp(uH)\big)_{p}, we have

ψ⁡(vp​x​w​P)=o⁡(vp​w)​|P|=ψ⁡(vp​w​P),ψ⁡(up​y​z​Q)=o⁡(up​z)​|Q|=ψ⁡(up​z​Q).\psi(v_{p}xwP)=o(v_{p}w)|P|=\psi(v_{p}wP),\qquad\psi(u_{p}yzQ)=o(u_{p}z)|Q|=\psi(u_{p}zQ).

Therefore,

ψ⁡(v​w​G)\displaystyle\psi(vwG) =(p−1)​ψ​(v​w​x​N)+ψ⁡(v​w​N)\displaystyle=(p-1)\psi(vwxN)+\psi(vwN)
=p​ψ​(v​w​N)\displaystyle=p\,\psi(vwN)
>p​ψ​(u​z​M)\displaystyle>p\,\psi(uzM)
OPEN=(p−1)​ψ​(u​y​z​M)+ψ⁡(u​z​M))\displaystyle=(p-1)\psi(uyzM)+\psi(uzM))
=ψ⁡(u​z​H).\displaystyle=\psi(uzH).

Now assume ψ⁡(v​x​N)>ψ⁡(u​y​M)\psi(vxN)>\psi(uyM). We show that ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)>\psi(uH). By Lemma 2.11,

o⁡(vp​x)=(exp⁡(v​G))p=(exp⁡(v​N))p,o⁡(up​y)=(exp⁡(u​H))p=(exp⁡(u​M))p.o(v_{p}x)=\big(\exp(vG)\big)_{p}=\big(\exp(vN)\big)_{p},\qquad o(u_{p}y)=\big(\exp(uH)\big)_{p}=\big(\exp(uM)\big)_{p}.

First assume ψ⁡(v​N)<ψ⁡(u​M)\psi(vN)<\psi(uM). Let w1=yw_{1}=y and z1=xz_{1}=x. By Lemma 2.12, o⁡(v​z1,N)=o⁡(v​z1)o(vz_{1},N)=o(vz_{1}) and o⁡(u​w1,M)=o⁡(u​w1)o(uw_{1},M)=o(uw_{1}). Since e​x​p​(v​N)=e​x​p​(v​G)exp(vN)=exp(vG) and e​x​p​(u​M)=e​x​p​(u​H)exp(uM)=exp(uH), we have o⁡(vp​z1)=(e​x​p​(v​N))po(v_{p}z_{1})=\big(exp(vN)\big)_{p} and o⁡(up​w1)=(e​x​p​(u​M))po(u_{p}w_{1})=\big(exp(uM)\big)_{p}. By the induction hypothesis,

ψ⁡(v​x​N)=ψ⁡(v​z1​N)<ψ⁡(u​w1​M)=ψ⁡(v​y​M),\psi(vxN)=\psi(vz_{1}N)<\psi(uw_{1}M)=\psi(vyM),

a contradiction. Thus ψ⁡(v​N)≥ψ⁡(u​M)\psi(vN)\geq\psi(uM), and hence

ψ⁡(v​G)=(p−1)​ψ​(v​x​N)+ψ⁡(v​N)>(p−1)​ψ​(u​y​M)+ψ⁡(u​M)=ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)=(p-1)\psi(vxN)+\psi(vN)>(p-1)\psi(uyM)+\psi(uM)=\psi(uH).

∎

Lemma 3.4.

Let G≤AG\leq A and H≤BH\leq B be finite ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM}-groups such that |G|=|H||G|=|H|. Let v∈Av\in A and u∈Bu\in B satisfy

o(v,G)=o(v),o(u,H)=o(u),andπ(o(v))=π(o(u)).o(v,G)=o(v),\qquad o(u,H)=o(u),\qquad\text{and}\qquad\pi(o(v))=\pi(o(u)).

Let M≤GM\leq G and N≤HN\leq H be maximal subgroups of index pp, chosen such that

ψ⁡(v​M)≤ψ⁡(v​R)andψ⁡(u​N)≤ψ⁡(u​E)\psi(vM)\leq\psi(vR)\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(uN)\leq\psi(uE)

for all maximal subgroups RR and EE of index pp in GG and HH, respectively. Assume moreover that exp⁡(v​M)=exp⁡(v​G)\exp(vM)=\exp(vG).

If ψ⁡(v⁡(G∖M))>ψ⁡(u⁡(H∖N)),\psi\big(v(G\setminus M)\big)>\psi\big(u(H\setminus N)\big), then ψ⁡(v​G)>ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)>\psi(uH).

Proof.

Let x∈G∖Nx\in G\setminus N and y∈H∖My\in H\setminus M satisfy o⁡(x)=o⁡(x,N)o(x)=o(x,N) and o⁡(y)=o⁡(y,M)o(y)=o(y,M).

If exp⁡(v​N)=exp⁡(v​G)\exp(vN)=\exp(vG) and exp⁡(u​M)=exp⁡(u​H)\exp(uM)=\exp(uH), then the result follows directly from Lemma 3.3. Hence, assume exp⁡(u​M)=exp⁡(u​H)/p\exp(uM)=\exp(uH)/p.

If ψ⁡(v​N)≥ψ⁡(u​M)\psi(vN)\geq\psi(uM), then

ψ⁡(v​G)=(p−1)​ψ​(v​x​N)+ψ⁡(v​N)>(p−1)​ψ​(u​y​M)+ψ⁡(u​M)=ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)=(p-1)\psi(vxN)+\psi(vN)>(p-1)\psi(uyM)+\psi(uM)=\psi(uH).

Now suppose ψ⁡(u​M)>ψ⁡(v​N)\psi(uM)>\psi(vN). Let P∈S​y​lp​(G)P\in Syl_{p}(G) and Q∈S​y​lp​(H)Q\in Syl_{p}(H). Since GG and HH are L​C​MLCM-groups, they are nilpotent, so

G=P×KandH=Q×F,G=P\times K\quad\text{and}\quad H=Q\times F,

where KK and FF are Hall p′p^{\prime}-subgroups of GG and HH, respectively.

Since exp⁡(v​N)=exp⁡(v​G)\exp(vN)=\exp(vG) and both ψ⁡(v​N)\psi(vN) and ψ⁡(u​M)\psi(uM) are minimal among all maximal subgroups of index pp of GG and HH, we have

o⁡(vp​x)=(exp⁡(v​G))pando⁡(up​y)=(exp⁡(u​H))p.o(v_{p}x)=\big(\exp(vG)\big)_{p}\quad\text{and}\quad o(u_{p}y)=\big(\exp(uH)\big)_{p}.

As exp⁡(u​M)=(exp⁡(u​H))p/p\exp(uM)=\big(\exp(uH)\big)_{p}/p, it follows that

ψ⁡(u​y​M)\displaystyle\psi(uyM) =o⁡(up​y)​|M∩Q|​ψ​(up′​F)\displaystyle=o(u_{p}y)|M\cap Q|\psi(u_{p^{\prime}}F)
=p⁡(o⁡(up​y)/p)​|M∩Q|​ψ​(up′​F)\displaystyle=p(o(u_{p}y)/p)|M\cap Q|\psi(u_{p^{\prime}}F)
≥p​ψ​(up​(M∩Q))​ψ​(up′​F)\displaystyle\geq p\psi(u_{p}(M\cap Q))\psi(u_{p^{\prime}}F)
=p​ψ​(u​M).\displaystyle=p\,\psi(uM).

On the other hand, since (exp⁡(v​N))p=o⁡(vp​x)\big(\exp(vN)\big)_{p}=o(v_{p}x), by Lemma 2.17 we have

p​ψ​(vp​x​N)\displaystyle p\,\psi(v_{p}xN) =p​ψ​(vp​x​(N∩P))​ψ​(vp′​K)\displaystyle=p\,\psi(v_{p}x(N\cap P))\psi(v_{p^{\prime}}K)
<(p+1)​ψ​(vp​(N∩P))​ψ​(vp′​K)\displaystyle<(p+1)\psi(v_{p}(N\cap P))\psi(v_{p^{\prime}}K)
=(p+1)​ψ​(v​N).\displaystyle=(p+1)\psi(vN).

Therefore,

ψ⁡(v​N)>pp+1​ψ​(v​x​N)>pp+1​ψ​(u​y​M)>p2p+1​ψ​(u​M)>ψ⁡(u​M),\psi(vN)>\frac{p}{p+1}\psi(vxN)>\frac{p}{p+1}\psi(uyM)>\frac{p^{2}}{p+1}\psi(uM)>\psi(uM),

which leads to a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Let G≤A∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\leq A\in\mathcal{LCM} be finite pp-groups, where A=⟨u⟩×GA=\langle u\rangle\times G for some u∈Au\in A. If RR and NN are two maximal subgroups of GG such that ψ⁡(R)≤ψ⁡(N)\psi(R)\leq\psi(N), then

ψ⁡(u​R)≤ψ⁡(u​N).\psi(uR)\leq\psi(uN).
Proof.

Let w∈R∖Nw\in R\setminus N and g∈N∖Rg\in N\setminus R such that

o⁡(w)=o⁡(w,N∩R),o⁡(g)=o⁡(g,N∩R).o(w)=o(w,N\cap R),\qquad o(g)=o(g,N\cap R).

By Lemma 2.11, for all z∈R∩Nz\in R\cap N, we have

o⁡(u​w​z)=l​c​m​(o⁡(u),o⁡(w),o⁡(z))ando⁡(u​g​z)=l​c​m​(o⁡(u),o⁡(g),o⁡(z)).o(uwz)=lcm(o(u),o(w),o(z))\quad\text{and}\quad o(ugz)=lcm(o(u),o(g),o(z)).

If o⁡(w)>o⁡(g)o(w)>o(g), then

ψ⁡(R)\displaystyle\psi(R) =(p−1)​ψ​(w⁡(R∩N))+ψ⁡(R∩N)\displaystyle=(p-1)\psi(w(R\cap N))+\psi(R\cap N)
>(p−1)​ψ​(g⁡(R∩N))+ψ⁡(R∩N)\displaystyle>(p-1)\psi(g(R\cap N))+\psi(R\cap N)
=ψ⁡(N),\displaystyle=\psi(N),

which contradicts our assumption. So o⁡(w)≤o⁡(g).o(w)\leq o(g). Then

ψ⁡(u​R)\displaystyle\psi(uR) =(p−1)​ψ​(u​w​(R∩N))+ψ⁡(u⁡(R∩N))\displaystyle=(p-1)\psi(uw(R\cap N))+\psi(u(R\cap N))
≤(p−1)​ψ​(u​g​(R∩N))+ψ⁡((u​R∩N))\displaystyle\leq(p-1)\psi(ug(R\cap N))+\psi((uR\cap N))
=ψ⁡(u​N).\displaystyle=\psi(uN).

∎

Theorem 3.6.

Let G≤AG\leq A and H≤BH\leq B be two finite L​C​MLCM-groups such that |G|=|H|=n|G|=|H|=n.

Let v∈Av\in A and u∈Bu\in B be two pp-elements such that

o⁡(v)=o⁡(v,G)≥pr​(e​x​p​(G))p,o⁡(u,H)=o⁡(u)≤pr​(e​x​p​(H))p,o(v)=o(v,G)\geq p^{r}\big(exp(G)\big)_{p},\quad o(u,H)=o(u)\leq p^{r}\big(exp(H)\big)_{p},

and π⁡(o⁡(v))=π⁡(o⁡(u)).\pi(o(v))=\pi(o(u)). If ψ⁡(G)≥ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)\geq\psi(H), then ψ⁡(v​G)≥ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)\geq\psi(uH).

Proof.

We argue by double induction on the ordered pair (o⁡(v),n)(o(v),n), where n=|G|n=|G|, ordered lexicographically.

Base of induction.

First suppose that o⁡(v)=1o(v)=1. Then v=1v=1, and since π⁡(o⁡(v))=π⁡(o⁡(u))=∅\pi(o(v))=\pi(o(u))=\varnothing, we also have u=1u=1. Hence

ψ⁡(v​G)=ψ⁡(G)≥ψ⁡(H)=ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)=\psi(G)\geq\psi(H)=\psi(uH).

Therefore, the statement holds for all pairs (1,n)(1,n) with n≥1n\geq 1.

Now assume that o⁡(v)≥po(v)\geq p, so that

π⁡(o⁡(v))={p}=π⁡(o⁡(u)).\pi(o(v))=\{p\}=\pi(o(u)).

Consequently, o⁡(u)≥po(u)\geq p.

If n=1n=1, then GG and HH are the trivial subgroups of AA and BB, respectively. Thus

ψ⁡(v​G)=o⁡(v)andψ⁡(u​H)=o⁡(u).\psi(vG)=o(v)\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(uH)=o(u).

Since o⁡(v)≥pr≥o⁡(u)o(v)\geq p^{r}\geq o(u), we obtain

ψ⁡(v​G)≥ψ⁡(u​H).\psi(vG)\geq\psi(uH).

Hence, the statement holds for all pairs (o⁡(v),1)(o(v),1).

Induction step.

Let G1≤A1G_{1}\leq A_{1} and H1≤B1H_{1}\leq B_{1} be finite L​C​MLCM-groups such that

|G1|=|H1|=n1.|G_{1}|=|H_{1}|=n_{1}.

Let v1∈A1v_{1}\in A_{1} and u1∈B1u_{1}\in B_{1} be pp-elements satisfying

o⁡(v1)=o⁡(v1,G1)≥pr1​(exp⁡(G1))p,o(v_{1})=o(v_{1},G_{1})\geq p^{r_{1}}\big(\exp(G_{1})\big)_{p},
o⁡(u1)=o⁡(u1,H1)≤pr1​(exp⁡(H1))p,o(u_{1})=o(u_{1},H_{1})\leq p^{r_{1}}\big(\exp(H_{1})\big)_{p},

Theorem 3.7.

Let N≤GN\leq G and M≤HM\leq H be finite ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM}-groups of the same order and suppose [G:N]=[H:M]=p[G:N]=[H:M]=p is a prime number. Assume ψ⁡(N)\psi(N) and ψ⁡(M)\psi(M) are minimal among all maximal subgroups of index pp of GG and HH, respectively. If ψ⁡(G∖N)>ψ⁡(H∖M)\psi(G\setminus N)>\psi(H\setminus M), then ψ⁡(G)>ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)>\psi(H).

Proof.

Choose x∈G∖Nx\in G\setminus N and y∈H∖My\in H\setminus M with o⁡(x)=o⁡(x,N)o(x)=o(x,N) and o⁡(y)=o⁡(y,M)o(y)=o(y,M). By Lemma 2.11, we have

o⁡(x)=(exp⁡(G))pando⁡(y)=(exp⁡(H))p.o(x)=\big(\exp(G)\big)_{p}\qquad\text{and}\qquad o(y)=\big(\exp(H)\big)_{p}.

Since

ψ⁡(G∖N)=(p−1)​ψ​(x​N)andψ⁡(H∖M)=(p−1)​ψ​(y​M),\psi(G\setminus N)=(p-1)\psi(xN)\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(H\setminus M)=(p-1)\psi(yM),

the hypothesis ψ⁡(G∖N)>ψ⁡(H∖M)\psi(G\setminus N)>\psi(H\setminus M) implies

ψ⁡(x​N)>ψ⁡(y​M).\psi(xN)>\psi(yM).

If ψ⁡(N)≥ψ⁡(M)\psi(N)\geq\psi(M) then

ψ⁡(G)=(p−1)​ψ​(x​N)+ψ⁡(N)>(p−1)​ψ​(y​M)+ψ⁡(M)=ψ⁡(H),\psi(G)=(p-1)\psi(xN)+\psi(N)>(p-1)\psi(yM)+\psi(M)=\psi(H),

and we are done. Hence we may assume ψ⁡(N)<ψ⁡(M)\psi(N)<\psi(M).

If exp⁡(H)=exp⁡(M)\exp(H)=\exp(M) then, by Lemma 3.4, we would have ψ⁡(x​N)<ψ⁡(y​M)\psi(xN)<\psi(yM), contradicting ψ⁡(x​N)>ψ⁡(y​M)\psi(xN)>\psi(yM). Therefore exp⁡(M)=exp⁡(H)/p\exp(M)=\exp(H)/p.

If exp⁡(N)=exp⁡(G)/p\exp(N)=\exp(G)/p, then Theorem 3.6 yields ψ⁡(x​N)≤ψ⁡(y​M)\psi(xN)\leq\psi(yM), again a contradiction. Thus exp⁡(N)=exp⁡(G)\exp(N)=\exp(G).

By Lemma 2.17 we have the bound

ψ⁡(x​N)<p+1p​ψ​(N).\psi(xN)<\frac{p+1}{p}\,\psi(N).

Write H=Q×FH=Q\times F where Q∈Sylp​(H)Q\in\mathrm{Syl}_{p}(H) and FF is a Hall p′p^{\prime}-subgroup of HH. Since exp⁡(M)=exp⁡(H)/p\exp(M)=\exp(H)/p, a routine computation gives

ψ⁡(y​M)=ψ⁡(y⁡(Q∩M))​ψ​(F)≥p​ψ​(M).\psi(yM)=\psi\big(y(Q\cap M)\big)\,\psi(F)\geq p\,\psi(M).

Combining the inequalities we obtain

ψ⁡(N)>pp+1​ψ​(x​N)≥pp+1​ψ​(y​M)≥p2p+1​ψ​(M).\psi(N)>\frac{p}{p+1}\psi(xN)\geq\frac{p}{p+1}\psi(yM)\geq\frac{p^{2}}{p+1}\psi(M).

But p2p+1>1\dfrac{p^{2}}{p+1}>1 for every prime p≥2p\geq 2, so the last chain implies ψ⁡(N)>ψ⁡(M)\psi(N)>\psi(M), contradicting our assumption ψ⁡(N)<ψ⁡(M)\psi(N)<\psi(M).

This contradiction shows the assumption ψ⁡(G∖N)>ψ⁡(H∖M)\psi(G\setminus N)>\psi(H\setminus M) forces ψ⁡(G)>ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)>\psi(H), as claimed. ∎

Now, we can prove the Theorem 1.3.

Theorem 3.8.

Let GG and HH be finite ℒ​𝒞​ℳ\mathcal{LCM}-groups of the same order. Then ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H) if and only if GG and HH have the same order type.

Proof.

(⇐\Leftarrow) Suppose GG and HH have the same order type. Then there exists a bijection f:G→Hf\colon G\to H such that o⁡(g)=o⁡(f⁡(g))o(g)=o(f(g)) for all g∈Gg\in G. Hence,

ψ⁡(G)=∑g∈Go⁡(g)=∑g∈Go⁡(f⁡(g))=ψ⁡(H).\psi(G)=\sum_{g\in G}o(g)=\sum_{g\in G}o(f(g))=\psi(H).

(⇒\Rightarrow) Conversely, assume ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H). We proceed by induction on |G||G|.

If GG is a pp-group, then by Lemma 3.1, GG and HH have the same order type.

So GG is not a pp-group. If for every non-trivial π\pi-Hall subgroups Gπ<GG_{\pi}<G and Hπ<HH_{\pi}<H we have ψ⁡(Gπ)=ψ⁡(Hπ)\psi(G_{\pi})=\psi(H_{\pi}), then the result follows by induction. Thus, we may suppose there for any π\pi-Hall subgroups Gπ≤GG_{\pi}\leq G and Hπ≤HH_{\pi}\leq H we have ψ⁡(Gπ)≠ψ⁡(Hπ)\psi(G_{\pi})\neq\psi(H_{\pi}).

Let pp be a prime divisor of |G||G|. Let P∈S​y​lp​(G)P\in Syl_{p}(G), Q∈S​y​lp​(H)Q\in Syl_{p}(H). Then G=P×Gp′G=P\times G_{p^{\prime}} and H=Q×Hp′H=Q\times H_{p^{\prime}} where where Gp′G_{p^{\prime}} and Hp′H_{p^{\prime}} be the p′p^{\prime}-Hall subgroups for GG and HH, respectively. Let M≤GM\leq G and N≤HN\leq H be maximal subgroups of index pp, chosen such that ψ⁡(v​M)\psi(vM) and ψ⁡(u​N)\psi(uN) are minimal among all maximal subgroups of index pp in GG and HH, respectively. By Theorem 3.7, ψ⁡(G∖N)=ψ⁡(H∖M).\psi(G\setminus N)=\psi(H\setminus M). Since

ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(G∖N)+ψ⁡(N)=ψ⁡(H∖M)+ψ⁡(M)=ψ⁡(H),\psi(G)=\psi(G\setminus N)+\psi(N)=\psi(H\setminus M)+\psi(M)=\psi(H),

we conclude that ψ⁡(N)=ψ⁡(M)\psi(N)=\psi(M). Thus, by the induction hypothesis, MM and NN have the same order type, so ψ⁡(Gp′)=ψ⁡(Hp′)\psi(G_{p^{\prime}})=\psi(H_{p^{\prime}}), which yields the final contradiction.

∎

The following theorem shows that for finite abelian groups, the notions of isomorphism, having the same order type, and having equal sums of element orders are all equivalent. In particular, it completely resolves Conjecture 1.1.

Theorem 3.9.

Let GG and HH be two finite abelian groups of order nn. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    The invariant factors of GG and HH are the same.

  2. (ii)

    G≅HG\cong H.

  3. (iii)

    GG and HH have the same order type.

  4. (iv)

    ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H).

Proof.

We prove the equivalences in a natural sequence.

(i)⇒(i​i)(i)\Rightarrow(ii), (i​i)⇒(i)(ii)\Rightarrow(i) and (i​i)⇒(i​i​i)(ii)\Rightarrow(iii) are immediate.

(i​i​i)⇒(i​i)(iii)\Rightarrow(ii): Decompose

G=P1×⋯×Pk,H=Q1×⋯×Qk,G=P_{1}\times\cdots\times P_{k},\qquad H=Q_{1}\times\cdots\times Q_{k},

where Pi∈Sylpi⁡(G)P_{i}\in\operatorname{Syl}_{p_{i}}(G) and Qi∈Sylpi⁡(H)Q_{i}\in\operatorname{Syl}_{p_{i}}(H) for each i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k.

Since GG and HH have the same order type, each pair of corresponding Sylow pip_{i}-subgroups PiP_{i} and QiQ_{i} also have the same order type. Let f:Pi→Qif:P_{i}\to Q_{i} be a bijection such that o⁡(x)=o⁡(f⁡(x))o(x)=o(f(x)) for all x∈Pix\in P_{i}. Then

ψ⁡(Pi)=∑x∈Pio⁡(x)=∑x∈Pio⁡(f⁡(x))=ψ⁡(Qi).\psi(P_{i})=\sum_{x\in P_{i}}o(x)=\sum_{x\in P_{i}}o(f(x))=\psi(Q_{i}).

By Corollary 3.2, it follows that Pi≅QiP_{i}\cong Q_{i} for all ii. Consequently,

G≅P1×⋯×Pk≅Q1×⋯×Qk≅H.G\cong P_{1}\times\cdots\times P_{k}\;\cong\;Q_{1}\times\cdots\times Q_{k}\cong H.

(i​i​i)⇔(i​v)(iii)\Leftrightarrow(iv) It follows from Theorem 3.8.

Thus all four statements are equivalent. ∎

In view of Theorem 3.8, the following question naturally arises.

Question 3.10.

Let G∈ℒ​𝒞​ℳG\in\mathcal{LCM} and HH be two finite groups of the same order with exp⁡(H)|exp⁡(G)\exp(H)\mid\exp(G).

  1. (1)

    If ψ⁡(G)=ψ⁡(H)\psi(G)=\psi(H), must GG and HH necessarily have the same order type?

  2. (2)

    If H∉ℒ​𝒞​ℳH\not\in\mathcal{LCM}, is it true that ψ⁡(H)<ψ⁡(G)\psi(H)<\psi(G)?
